title: How Does a Heat Pump Work? A Plain Explanation
h1: How Does a Heat Pump Work for Heating and Cooling?
description: A heat pump moves heat instead of making it. Here's how it heats and cools a San Diego or Orange County home, and what to expect day to day.
quick_answer: A heat pump moves heat rather than creating it. In winter it pulls heat out of the outdoor air and releases it inside. In summer it reverses and pulls heat out of your house, working like an air conditioner. One outdoor unit and one indoor unit handle both jobs, powered by electricity instead of gas.
body:
What is a heat pump, in simple terms?

A heat pump is an air conditioner that can run in reverse. It has the same basic parts as a central AC: an outdoor unit with a compressor and coil, an indoor coil, and refrigerant lines connecting them. The difference is a small part called a reversing valve, which lets the system change the direction the refrigerant flows.

Because it moves existing heat from one place to another, a heat pump can deliver more heat energy than the electricity it uses. That's the main reason people choose one over electric resistance heat like baseboard heaters or a plain electric furnace.

How does a heat pump heat a house?

Even cool outdoor air holds heat. The refrigerant in the outdoor coil is colder than the outside air, so it absorbs that heat. Here's the sequence on a winter night:

  1. Cold, low-pressure refrigerant in the outdoor coil soaks up heat from the outside air.
  2. The compressor squeezes that refrigerant, which raises its pressure and temperature.
  3. The hot refrigerant travels to the indoor coil, usually in an air handler in the attic, garage or a hall closet.
  4. The indoor blower pushes house air across that warm coil and out through your ducts.
  5. The refrigerant gives up its heat, cools down, passes through an expansion device and heads back outside to start again.

The air coming out of the registers feels warm but not as hot as air from a gas furnace. A heat pump tends to run longer, gentler cycles. That's normal and usually feels more even.

How does it cool in the summer?

In cooling mode, the reversing valve flips the flow. Now the indoor coil is the cold side. It absorbs heat from the air in your house, and the outdoor unit dumps that heat outside. The indoor coil also pulls moisture out of the air as it cools, which helps on muggy coastal days.

From the homeowner's side, it works exactly like central air. You set the thermostat to cool and the system does the rest.

What about defrost mode and backup heat?

On cold, damp mornings the outdoor coil can pick up frost. The system handles this with a defrost cycle. It briefly switches to cooling mode to warm the outdoor coil and melt the ice. You may see steam rising from the outdoor unit and hear a whoosh when the valve shifts. Both are normal.

Many heat pumps also have backup heat strips in the air handler, sometimes called auxiliary or emergency heat. They kick in during defrost or when the heat pump can't keep up on its own. If your thermostat shows aux heat running often on mild days, have the system checked, because those strips use a lot more electricity than the heat pump itself.

Do heat pumps work well in Southern California?

Our climate suits them. Coastal winters are mild, and even inland valleys with chilly nights rarely get cold enough to push a modern heat pump past what it can handle. The same unit also covers hot inland summers, so one system replaces both a furnace and an AC.

A few local things to keep in mind:

  • Salt air near the coast can corrode outdoor coils and fins. Rinsing the outdoor unit gently with a hose and keeping up with tune-ups helps.
  • Attic air handlers are common in older stucco tract homes. Leaky or poorly insulated attic ducts waste heat in winter and cooling in summer.
  • Santa Ana winds and wildfire smoke load up filters fast. Check yours more often during those stretches.

What kinds of heat pumps are there?

Most homes use one of three setups:

  • Ducted split heat pump: an outdoor unit paired with an indoor air handler and your existing ducts. This is the usual swap for an old furnace and AC.
  • Ductless mini-split: an outdoor unit feeding one or more wall-mounted heads. Good for additions, garages converted to living space, or homes without ducts.
  • Dual fuel (hybrid): a heat pump paired with a gas furnace. The heat pump handles most of the heating, and the furnace takes over when it's more practical.

Which one fits depends on your ducts, your electrical panel, and how the house is laid out. Our heating team can look at your home and lay out the options with a free estimate.

How do you keep a heat pump running well?

Change or clean the filter on schedule, keep plants and debris a couple of feet away from the outdoor unit, and don't block indoor return grilles. Because a heat pump works year-round instead of just one season, a professional tune-up once a year, or twice if you run it hard, catches refrigerant, electrical and airflow issues early. Leave refrigerant and electrical work to a technician.
faqs: Is a heat pump the same as an air conditioner?

Mechanically they're very close. A heat pump has the same compressor, coils and refrigerant lines as a central AC, plus a reversing valve that lets it run backward to heat the house. An AC only cools.
Why is cool air coming out when my heat pump is on heat?

During a defrost cycle the system briefly switches to cooling to melt frost off the outdoor coil, so you may feel cooler air for a few minutes. If it lasts longer than that, check the thermostat setting and the filter, then call for service.
Do I need a gas line for a heat pump?
No. A heat pump runs on electricity. If you're replacing a gas furnace, the gas line can be capped by a qualified technician, or kept for a dual fuel setup that pairs a heat pump with a furnace.
How long does a heat pump last?

It depends on the equipment, installation quality and how well it's maintained. Because it runs in both summer and winter, it gets more hours of use than an AC that only cools, so regular tune-ups matter more.
